questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Congress Dominance in the First Three General Elections' refers to.
questions.a: The Indian National Congress won overwhelming majorities in the Lok Sabha in the first three general elections (1952, 1957, 1962), establishing a system of one-party dominance that was distinct from a one-party system because free and fair elections were held and opposition parties operated legally.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Congress Dominance in the First Three General Elections'.
questions.a: Congress dominance rested on its organisational reach, its legacy of the freedom struggle, and its ability to absorb diverse social groups, making it the natural ruling party of the post-independence period.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Congress Dominance in the First Three General Elections' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nature of Congress Organisation' refers to.
questions.a: The Congress functioned as a broad umbrella organisation that contained within it groups with divergent ideological positions, often described as the 'Congress system' where the party acted as a forum for negotiation among internal factions.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nature of Congress Organisation'.
questions.a: The Congress was not a unified, ideologically coherent party but a coalition of factions -- the left, the right, and the centre -- that contested elections and debated policy within a single organisational framework.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nature of Congress Organisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Congress as a Social Coalition' refers to.
questions.a: The Congress derived its strength from a social coalition that included upper castes, peasants, the landed classes, industrialists, and sections of the working class and minorities, allowing it to represent a wide cross-section of Indian society.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Congress as a Social Coalition'.
questions.a: The Congress was a social coalition because it drew support from diverse caste, class, religious, and regional groups, and its organisational structure allowed local elites from different social strata to participate in the party.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Congress as a Social Coalition' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Role of Opposition Parties' refers to.
questions.a: Opposition parties in the 1950s and 1960s were weak in terms of seats but played a crucial role in maintaining the democratic character of the polity by articulating alternative visions, criticising the government, and keeping alive a competitive party system.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Role of Opposition Parties'.
questions.a: Even though opposition parties won few seats, their presence ensured that the Congress did not become authoritarian, and they kept alive ideological alternatives that would later mature into viable challengers.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Role of Opposition Parties' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Socialist Party' refers to.
questions.a: The Socialist Party was formed in 1948 by leaders who believed that the Congress was becoming a party of the propertied classes and that a separate socialist party was needed to pursue democratic socialism, land reforms, and workers' rights.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Socialist Party'.
questions.a: The Socialist Party represented the democratic socialist tradition in Indian politics, advocating land reforms, cooperative farming, and workers' rights, but it suffered from factionalism and could not build a durable electoral base.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Socialist Party' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Communist Party of India' refers to.
questions.a: The Communist Party of India (CPI) was founded in 1925 and, after independence, emerged as the main opposition party in the first general elections, winning 16 seats and performing strongly in states like Kerala, Andhra, and West Bengal.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Communist Party of India'.
questions.a: The CPI combined a Marxist ideological framework with electoral participation, and its strong regional bases in Kerala, Andhra, and West Bengal made it the most successful opposition party of the period, though internal ideological debates over the path to socialism led to splits.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Communist Party of India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Bharatiya Jana Sangh' refers to.
questions.a: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in 1951 by Shyama Prasad Mukherjee with the support of the RSS and represented the Hindu nationalist tradition in Indian politics, advocating a strong and united India, the abolition of Article 370, and a pro-Hindi, pro-market economic programme.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bharatiya Jana Sangh'.
questions.a: The Jana Sangh represented the right-wing alternative to the Congress, drawing its ideological inspiration from the RSS and advocating Hindu nationalism, cultural nationalism, and a market-oriented economy, though its electoral base remained limited in the 1950s and 1960s.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Bharatiya Jana Sangh' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Swatantra Party' refers to.
questions.a: The Swatantra Party was formed in 1959 by C. Rajagopalachari, N. G. Ranga, and Minoo Masani in reaction to the increasing state control and socialist orientation of the Congress, advocating free enterprise, a reduction in state regulation, and the protection of private property.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Swatantra Party'.
questions.a: The Swatantra Party represented the classical liberal and conservative critique of the Congress's socialist and statist policies, arguing for free markets, reduced government intervention, and the protection of fundamental rights, and drew support from landlords, princes, and business interests.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Swatantra Party' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Elections and Democracy in the Early Years' refers to.
questions.a: The conduct of regular, free, and fair elections based on universal adult franchise from 1952 onwards established the institutional foundation of Indian democracy, even though the Congress dominated the outcomes, and the elections produced a competitive party system that deepened over time.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Elections and Democracy in the Early Years'.
questions.a: The first three general elections demonstrated that a large, poor, and largely illiterate society could sustain democratic elections based on universal adult franchise, and that elections created a competitive political culture even under one-party dominance.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Elections and Democracy in the Early Years' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance
